content: Whey protein refers to a group of globular proteins that are derived from whey, a by-product of cheese production using cow's milk. It is primarily composed of beta-lactoglobulin (~65%), alpha-lactalbumin (~25%), and serum albumin (~8%), all of which remain soluble in their native forms regardless of pH levels. Whey protein is notable for having the highest Biological Value (BV) among all known proteins, indicating its superior ability to provide essential amino acids for human nutrition. Whey protein is either lactose-free or contains reduced lactose and is rich in various nutrients and essential amino acids. It consists of four major protein fractions—beta-lactoglobulin, alpha-lactalbumin, bovine serum albumin, and immunoglobulins—as well as six minor protein fractions. These components are known to have significant disease-fighting properties. Additionally, whey protein is highly digestible and does not aggregate when milk is subjected to renneting or acidification under normal conditions. However, when exposed to heat or acidic environments, whey proteins may partially unfold, leading to hydrophobic interactions with other proteins and the formation of disulfide bonds with casein micelles, resulting in aggregation at low pH levels. Whey protein can undergo denaturation, an irreversible structural change caused by heat, similar to the transformation of egg whites from a clear liquid to a white solid when cooked. High heat, such as the sustained temperatures above 72°C (160°F) used in pasteurization, can denature whey proteins, reducing their bioactive compounds, including cysteine, an amino acid critical for the synthesis of glutathione, a potent antioxidant. Whey protein is available in three primary forms: concentrate, isolate, and hydrolysate. Whey protein concentrates contain low levels of fat and cholesterol but retain higher levels of bioactive compounds and carbohydrates in the form of lactose, with protein content ranging from 29% to 89% by weight. Isolates are processed to remove fat and lactose, resulting in a protein content of over 90% by weight, though they generally have fewer bioactive compounds. Hydrolysates are pre-digested, partially hydrolyzed whey proteins that are more easily absorbed by the body but are typically more expensive. Whey protein is widely used for its nutritional benefits. It contains high levels of both essential and non-essential amino acids, making it a valuable dietary supplement. Pregnant women are sometimes advised by their obstetricians to include whey protein in their diets to ensure their developing babies receive all necessary amino acids. Whey protein powder is also popular among bodybuilders and athletes for promoting muscle growth and aiding recovery. Individuals with compromised or abnormal immune systems, as well as those with degenerative diseases, may use undenatured bioactive whey proteins to boost their antioxidant levels. Undenatured whey proteins are an excellent source of cysteine, a conditionally essential amino acid that plays a key role in the body's production of glutathione. Commercial whey protein products are widely available in health food stores and supermarket health sections. These products often consist of isolate/concentrate blends or isolate/concentrate/hydrolysate mixtures and are typically flavored for easy mixing with water or milk to create shakes or drinks. Despite their perceived cost, whey protein supplements can often be purchased affordably from reputable sports stores.
